landing.lede: A query you register is a question the engine keeps answering. Not a job you submit and wait on — a view that is already correct when you read it, maintained row by row as the data arrives, and shared by everyone who asked the same thing.

name.title: pravāha — that which flows
name.p1_flow: : a river's flow, continuous and directional. Not the water, which is always different water — the
name.p1_after: , which is the thing that persists.
name.p2: Which is what a stream is, and what makes streaming hard to reason about. The rows are gone the moment they pass. What you keep is the answer they changed, and the discipline is knowing which answers a row can still change and which it cannot.
name.p3_question: can anything still arrive that changes this?
name.p3_after: — is what watermarks answer, what retention rests on, and what decides when a window may close.

different.incremental_body: A change is a delta. Z-sets carry weights, so a correction is a retraction and an insert — never a rescan.
different.event_time_body: A window closes when the data says it is over, not when the clock does. Late rows correct the answer rather than being lost.
different.shared_body: Two people asking the same question get one computation and one copy of the state — matched on the normalised plan, not the SQL text.
different.bounded_body: Every operator that could grow without limit has a bound, and a query with no bound is refused at plan time rather than at 3am.

does.continuous_body: Register SQL under a name. The engine maintains its view for as long as it is registered, and clients read or subscribe.
does.joins_body: Two streams joined on a key and a time bound — including LEFT, where the unmatched row is emitted once the window has passed.
does.protocol_body: Arrow Flight SQL for query, prepare, register and subscribe. Both SDKs and the CLI speak it; so does any Flight client.
does.answers_body: A view is already computed when you ask. There is no serving database because the serving database is not needed.

diagram.title: How Pravaha works
diagram.desc: Rows from your stores feed declared streams. A continuous query, registered once, turns every change into a Z-set delta and maintains a keyed view. The view is read by key, subscribed to commit by commit, or written to a sink. Checkpoints and the registry journal let a restart resume.

how.1: A stream is declared — its schema, which column is event time, how late its rows may arrive — and bound to a source plugin that reads one of your stores.
how.2: A continuous query is registered once, under a name and a key. Calcite parses and plans it; Pravaha's own operators run it, as generated code, on a lane — and identical questions share one computation.
how.3: Every row becomes a change with a weight: +1 for a row appearing, −1 for one withdrawn. Operators transform changes into changes, so the work is proportional to what changed.
how.4: The watermark — how far event time has certainly advanced — closes windows. A late row inside the allowed lateness reopens a window as a retraction of the old answer and the corrected one, in one commit.
how.5: The view is the answer, maintained and keyed. Applications read it by key over Flight SQL or the PostgreSQL wire protocol, subscribe to its commits, or have the node write each commit to a sink. Checkpoints cut every input at one point, so a restart resumes.
